title: Trout Stocking Locations in Tennessee
description_raw: This service maps trout stocking locations throughout Tennessee, detailing stocking programs, species, access, and management authorities for statewide fisheries support. Overview This feature service provides detailed geographic information about trout stocking locations managed by various entities within the state of Tennessee. It is intended to serve anglers, wildlife managers, and conservationists interested in trout fisheries. Feature Layer Trout_MASTER_Project: This layer contains point features representing trout stocking sites including streams, ponds, and reservoirs across Tennessee. The data includes precise geographic coordinates and site-specific details such as site name, stream name, region, county, and city. Each site records key attributes such as the stocking program season (e.g., Spring, Winter), water type (stream, pond, reservoir), and species stocked (Rainbow, Brook, Brown, or combinations thereof). Additional management information is provided, including ownership or management authority (e.g., Private Land, USFS, TVA), access information such as 24-hour availability, sunrise/sunset accessibility, and parking facilities. Geographic Coverage The dataset covers multiple regions throughout Tennessee, including various counties and municipalities, providing comprehensive statewide coverage for trout stocking efforts. Potential Applications Supporting recreational fishing by identifying stocked trout locations and access details. Assisting wildlife and fisheries management in monitoring and planning stocking activities. Enabling environmental and conservation research related to freshwater ecosystems in Tennessee.

title: Tennessee River Miles and County Boundaries

title: Tennessee Conservation Opportunity Areas and Species of Greatest Conservation Need 2025
description_raw: Boundaries of Conservation Opportunity Areas and listings of Species of Greatest Conservation Need for Tennessee's 2025 State Wildlife Action Plan revision. Overview This feature service provides geographic and species data supporting Tennessee's 2025 State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) revision. It includes delineations of Conservation Opportunity Areas (COAs) across Tennessee and associated data on Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) within these regions. Feature Layers Conservation Opportunity Areas (TN_COA25): This layer represents the boundaries of 36 distinct Conservation Opportunity Areas identified in the 2025 revision of Tennessee's SWAP. The areas are geographically defined polygons used for targeted conservation efforts and wildlife management planning. Species of Greatest Conservation Need by COA (SGCNbyCOA2025): This table catalogs species considered critical for conservation, listing their taxonomic group, common and scientific names, and occurrence within each COA. It supports understanding species distribution and priorities within the designated conservation areas. Geographic Coverage The data covers the State of Tennessee, USA, focusing on regions important for conservation planning as designated by the state's wildlife authorities. Use Cases Wildlife conservation planning and prioritization by state agencies and conservation organizations. Supporting environmental assessments and habitat management decisions. Research and monitoring of at-risk species distribution within key conservation areas. Data Source and Management All data are provided and maintained by the Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency as part of the State Wildlife Action Plan 2025 revision initiative. The service facilitates data access for stakeholders involved in wildlife management and conservation.

title: Paddling Access Sites
description_raw: This service maps Tennessee's paddling access sites, detailing facilities, amenities, and access information for statewide recreational water use. Ownership and management information is provided to clarify jurisdictional responsibilities. Assisting governmental and resource agencies in managing boat ramps, marinas, and public water access points. Informing the public and stakeholders about locations, facilities, and services available at each site. Enabling spatial analyses related to waterway accessibility, facility distribution, and regional outdoor recreation planning.

title: Marina Sites
description_raw: This service features detailed data on Tennessee marinas, including amenities, parking, and access information for statewide recreational use. Overview This feature service provides comprehensive data on marinas located throughout the state of Tennessee. It is designed to support recreational boating and fishing activities by offering detailed information about facilities and amenities available across various public access points to waterways. Key features covered include: Location and type of access sites such as boat launches, marinas, and fishing sites. Parking details including surface type and capacity, including trailer parking. Facilities and amenities like gas availability, ice, bait, camping, restrooms, fishing piers, fish cleaning stations, and courtesy docks. Operational considerations such as access hours, seasonal closures, and 24-hour availability. Site ownership and management information by various government and private entities. Accessibility features including handicap and lighted parking. Restrictions or special conditions such as trolling-only areas or rental availability. Geographic Coverage The dataset covers the entire state of Tennessee, with sites organized by county and waterway, providing statewide access to boating facilities. Use Cases Planning and management of recreational boating and fishing infrastructure by state and local agencies. Providing the public with detailed site information for trip planning and safe boating access. Supporting emergency response and maintenance scheduling for water access points.

title: Fish Attractor Locations for Habitat Enhancement and Angler Access
description_raw: This service maps fish attractor locations with detailed habitat types and angler access information to support fisheries management and recreational fishing. Overview This feature service provides detailed spatial data on fish attractor locations designed to support fisheries habitat restoration, enhancement, and recreational fishing activities. The data primarily covers freshwater bodies, likely within the Tennessee region and surrounding areas based on spatial extent, aiming to inform habitat management and angler accessibility. Feature Layer FishAttractorLocations: This primary layer represents individual fish attractor sites, including a variety of natural, artificial, and live attractor types. The dataset captures geographic coordinates, elevation, depth, and site characteristics such as development stage and angler access. Artificial structures include reef balls, PVC structures, pallets, stakes, spawning benches, and other common habitat enhancements. Natural attractors like rock piles and brush lines, as well as live vegetation types such as cypress trees and native grasses, are also recorded to provide an ecological context. Geographic Coverage The service covers a region defined approximately between longitudes -88.28 and -81.91 and latitudes 34.93 and 36.99, indicating a focus in the southern United States, potentially Tennessee and neighboring areas. Use Cases Supporting fisheries habitat restoration and monitoring efforts by providing accurate locations and details of fish attractors. Assisting anglers and resource managers in identifying accessible fishing sites with various types of habitat features. Facilitating habitat assessment and management planning through attributes on site development, structure types, and cluster size.

description_raw: This NDVI imagery layer features recent high-resolution (1m or better) aerial imagery for the continental United States, made available by the USDA Farm Production and Conservation Business Center. This Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) layer features recent high-resolution (1-meter or better) aerial imagery for the continental United States, made available by the USDA Farm Production and Conservation Business Center (FPAC). The National Agriculture Imagery Program (NAIP) acquires aerial imagery during the agricultural growing seasons in the continental United States. Approximately half of the US is collected each year and each state is typically collected every other year. This imagery layer is updated annually as new imagery is made available. The NAIP program aims to make the imagery available to governmental agencies and to the public within a year of collection. The imagery is published in 4-bands (Red, Green, Blue, and Near Infrared) where available. Additional NAIP renderings include Natural Color and Color Infrared. Each processing template includes labels and descriptions to characterize the intended usage. This may include for visualization, for analysis, or for both visualization and analysis. Visualization The default rendering on this layer is NDVI ((Red - Near Infrared) / (Red + Near Infrared)). If natural color visualization is your primary use case for NAIP, you might consider using the NAIP Imagery tile layer for optimal display performance. There are a number of on-the-fly renderings/processing templates designed specifically for data visualization. By default, the most recent imagery available for a given area is prioritized and dynamically fused into a single mosaicked image layer. To discover and isolate specific images for visualization in Map Viewer, try using the Image Collection Explorer. Analysis In order to leverage the optimization for analysis, the capability must be enabled by your ArcGIS organization administrator. More information on enabling this feature can be found in the ‘Regional data hosting’ section of this help doc. Optimized for analysis means this layer does not have size constraints for analysis and it is recommended for multisource analysis with other layers optimized for analysis. See this group for a complete list of imagery layers optimized for analysis. Using the "None" processing template option as input to analysis provides all bands with raw pixel values and is recommended for many use cases. Otherwise, only processing templates that include a "for analysis" designation should be used as input to analysis. Prior to running analysis, users should always provide some form of data selection with either a layer filter (e.g. for a specific year, year range, state, etc.) or by selecting specific images. To discover and isolate specific images for analysis in Map Viewer, try using the Image Collection Explorer . title: Winter Storm Fern Damage Assessment
description_raw: Classified Winter Storm Fern damage assessment map service showing observed damage severity across Tennessee and portions of the central United States for storm review, imagery comparison, situational awareness, and recovery-related mapping. Winter Storm Fern HiForm Damage Assessment Overview This map service presents classified damage assessment information associated with Winter Storm Fern. The dataset supports visual review of storm-related impacts by displaying mapped damage classes across Tennessee. The service is intended for use with imagery comparison, storm damage review, regional assessment mapping, incident documentation, situational awareness, and recovery-related planning. In the Winter Storm Fern Imagery Swipe application, this layer can be viewed with post-storm imagery to compare mapped damage patterns against visible storm impacts. Map Service HiForm Damage Classes: This thematic raster layer represents classified storm damage conditions associated with Winter Storm Fern. The layer is displayed as a classified surface using category-based symbology. The raster layer was processed at a 12.5-meter spatial resolution, where each raster cell represents a classified damage condition. Damage Classes The layer includes the following damage classes: Little to No Damage Minimal Damage Moderate Damage Heavy Damage Severe Damage Data Characteristics This service visualizes a classified damage assessment surface where each pixel represents a mapped damage class value. The raster is delivered as a tiled map service to support efficient display, broad map access, and fast visualization across the regional assessment area. The layer is designed for visual interpretation and regional-scale damage review. It supports comparison with pre-storm and post-storm imagery, but it should not be interpreted as a parcel-level or site-specific damage determination. Additional information about HiForm high-resolution forest mapping and data processing methods is available from the U.S. Forest Service: https://research.fs.usda.gov/srs/products/dataandtools/high-resolution-forest-mapping-hiform Data Maintenance This layer represents a historical storm damage assessment associated with Winter Storm Fern. It is maintained as an event-specific mapping resource and may be updated if revised source data, corrected classifications, improved processing methods, or additional supporting information become available.

title: Traffic Points
description_raw: This point-layer stores traffic monitoring data such as historical AADTs, Class AADTs, and Truck Percentages. This dataset contains geospatial point data showing historical Annual Average Daily Traffic (AADT), Classification AADTs for all 13 FHWA classes, calculation methods for all AADTs, the Truck Percentage, and the TN-TIMES link for the station. The Calculation Method for the AADT indicates whether the Annual Average Daily Traffic was created directly from a raw count or if it calculated based on an alternate methodology: Actual – The AADT is based on an actual raw count from the given year. Grown – The AADT was grown from the previous year AADT based on the average growth rate of the county. AADTs calculated using this methodology have a superscript value 3 in TN-TIMES. Combined – The AADT was combined from two separate directional AADTs. Please refer to TN-TIMES for the directional AADT methodology. AADTs calculated using this methodology have a superscript value 7 in TN-TIMES. Doubled – The AADT was doubled from only one directional AADT. Please refer to TN-TIMES for the directional AADT methodology. AADTs calculated using this methodology have a superscript value 12 in TN-TIMES. Balanced – The AADT was calculated from corridor balancing. Corridor balancing is a method that relies on a start node on an interstate and adds and subtracts subsequent ramp volumes to calculate additional AADTs along the mainline. AADTs calculated using this methodology have a superscript value 8 in TN-TIMES. Virtual – The AADT was calculated based on a combination of related station AADTs. Please refer to TN-TIMES for the specific stations involved. AADTs calculated using this methodology have a superscript value 19 in TN-TIMES. The Calculation Method for the Class AADTs similarly indicates the source data for the value: Actual – The Class AADT is based on a raw class count collected at the station in the given year. Distributed – The Class AADTs are based on the average class distribution of the base stations that are in the same Class Distribution Group. The group assignment for the given station can be found in TN-TIMES. Derived – The Class AADTs are based on a combination of length data from the given station and the class distribution. Actual Class AADTs and Distributed Class AADTs are based on axle class counts rather than length counts. This dataset is updated annually.

title: Tennessee Wildfire Hazard Potential (Hexagon Grid)
description_raw: This service maps wildfire hazard potential across Tennessee using a hexagon-based spatial grid, supporting risk assessment and fire management efforts. Tennessee Wildfire Hazard Potential (Hexagon Grid) Overview This feature layer represents Wildfire Hazard Potential (WHP) across Tennessee using a statewide hexagonal grid system. The polygons in this dataset are 50-square-kilometer hexagon grids that provide a consistent spatial framework for identifying and analyzing areas where wildfire may be more difficult to manage. The data is derived from the USFS National Wildfire Hazard Potential dataset, produced by the USDA Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Research Station, with supporting wildfire hazard modeling from Pyrologix LLC. Wildfire Hazard Potential is an index that quantifies the relative potential for wildfire that may be difficult to manage and is commonly used to help prioritize where fuel treatments, mitigation efforts, and fire prevention strategies may be needed. This dataset is intended for use in wildfire risk assessment, forestry planning, fuel treatment prioritization, fire prevention planning, emergency management coordination, research, and public information purposes. It serves as a GIS reference layer for evaluating relative wildfire hazard patterns across Tennessee at a regional planning scale. Feature Layer WHP Hexagon Grids: This polygon layer represents 50-square-kilometer hexagon grid cells covering Tennessee. Each hexagon is associated with a Wildfire Hazard Potential classification and grid identification code. The layer provides a generalized spatial framework for analyzing relative wildfire hazard potential and supporting statewide wildfire planning, mitigation, and management activities. Data Attributes ClassCode: The Wildfire Hazard Potential classification assigned to the hexagon. Data Maintenance This layer is maintained by the TDF Forest Data and Analysis Unit. It is updated periodically as needed to reflect updated source data from the USFS National Wildfire Hazard Potential dataset, revised wildfire hazard modeling methods, improved source datasets, boundary refinements, or other administrative changes.

title: TN Scenic Rivers Lines
description_raw: Line feature class representing rivers or river segments designated as Tennessee Scenic Rivers. This line feature class contains rivers or river segments designated as Tennessee Scenic Rivers. The extents represented within do not constitute a survey product and are not legally binding. Limited attributes include river name, class designation, and calculated length where applicable. The data are updated twice per year (January and July) to reflect any changes made to the Act by the Tennessee General Assembly. For more information about Tennessee Scenic Rivers, visit the Tennessee Scenic Rivers Program web pages at https://www.tn.gov/environment/program-areas/na-natural-areas/tn-scenic-rivers.html. The Tennessee Scenic Rivers Program is intended to preserve and protect the free flowing, unpolluted and outstanding scenic, recreational, geologic, botanical, fish, wildlife, historic or cultural values of selected rivers or river segments in the state. Twenty-four rivers or segments of rivers are included in the state scenic rivers program. Program oversight is provided by the Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation (TDEC) in cooperation with the Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency (TWRA). Rivers are managed cooperatively with other state and federal agencies and non-governmental organizations following the standards outlined in the Tennessee Scenic Rivers Act of 1968 (Title 11; Chapter 13) and the Rules for the Management of Tennessee Natural Resource Areas. Tennessee has one river included in the National Wild and Scenic Rivers Program which is managed cooperatively with the National Park Service and follows the standards outlined in the National Wild and Scenic Rivers Act (Public Law 90-542; 16 U.S.C. 1271 et seq.).

title: Tennessee Forest Legacy Program Priority Areas (2020-2030)
description_raw: Tennessee Department of Agriculture, Division of Forestry updated priority areas for the Forest Legacy Program in its statewide Tennessee Forest Action Plan, 2020-2030. Visit our website to download a copy of the plan: https://www.tn.gov/agriculture/forests/protection/ag-forests-action-plan.html Tennessee Forest Legacy Program Priority Areas (2020-2030) The Tennessee Department of Agriculture, Division of Forestry updated priority areas for its Forest Legacy Program in the 2020 Tennessee Forest Action Plan. All 50 states are required by federal law to develop and update a Forest Action Plan every ten years in order to be eligible to receive funds under the Cooperative Forestry Assistance Act administered by the USDA Forest Service. This plan provides a comprehensive assessment of the condition of Tennessee's forest resources, risks and challenges associated with forest health and resiliency, and strategies for protecting, conserving, and enhancing this vital resource for our citizens and visitors. The 2020 Tennessee Forest Action Plan builds on the state's inaugural 2010 Forest Resource Assessment and Strategy. Implementation of the Forest Legacy Program fills an important gap and provides a safety net to protect environmentally important resources in Tennessee. Tennessee's Forest Legacy Program objectives are used to determine which eligible tracts will receive priority for participation in the program. Objectives are aimed at protecting forest resource values that stakeholders and public consider of greatest concern. The mission of Tennessee's Forest Legacy Program is to protect environmentally important, private forestlands threatened with conversion to non-forest uses. The primary focus of the program is to maintain well-managed, working forests. The objectives of Tennessee's Forest Legacy Program are as follows: Prevent conversion of forestland to other uses Preserve forestland for current and future wood production Preserve and protect water quality, fisheries, and water supplies Preserve and protect riparian habitats Preserve and protect fish and wildlife habitats, rare plants, and biological diversity Preserve and protect natural beauty Preserve and protect forest-based recreation opportunities Candidate properties must be forested tracts of at least 20 acres continuous forest and located in one of the top 60% of primary forest product-producing counties. Property must also be in a watershed with significant risk of becoming lightly stressed, stressed, impacted, or damaged due to extent of impervious surface by 2030, or at high risk of becoming urbanized by 2030. Finally, the property must be located within The Nature Conservancy's Resilient and Connected Prioritized Network. Tennessee's Forest Legacy Priority Areas dataset identifies areas that are currently eligible for the program.

This plan provides a comprehensive assessment of the condition of Tennessee's forest resources, risks and challenges associated with forest health and resiliency, and strategies for protecting, conserving, and enhancing this vital resource for our citizens and visitors. The 2020 Tennessee Forest Action Plan builds on the state's inaugural 2010 Forest Resource Assessment and Strategy. Implementation of the Forest Legacy Program fills an important gap and provides a safety net to protect environmentally important resources in Tennessee. Tennessee's Forest Legacy Program objectives are used to determine which eligible tracts will receive priority for participation in the program. Objectives are aimed at protecting forest resource values that stakeholders and public consider of greatest concern. The mission of Tennessee's Forest Legacy Program is to protect environmentally important, private forestlands threatened with conversion to non-forest uses. The primary focus of the program is to maintain well-managed, working forests. The objectives of Tennessee's Forest Legacy Program are as follows: Prevent conversion of forestland to other uses Preserve forestland for current and future wood production Preserve and protect water quality, fisheries, and water supplies Preserve and protect riparian habitats Preserve and protect fish and wildlife habitats, rare plants, and biological diversity Preserve and protect natural beauty Preserve and protect forest-based recreation opportunities Candidate properties must be forested tracts of at least 20 acres continuous forest and located in one of the top 60% of primary forest product-producing counties. Property must also be in a watershed with significant risk of becoming lightly stressed, stressed, impacted, or damaged due to extent of impervious surface by 2030, or at high risk of becoming urbanized by 2030. Finally, the property must be located within The Nature Conservancy's Resilient and Connected Prioritized Network. Tennessee's Forest Legacy Priority Areas dataset identifies areas that are currently eligible for the program.

title: National Wetlands Inventory
description_raw: The present goal of the Service is to provide the citizens of the United States and its Trust Territories with current geospatially referenced information on the status, extent, characteristics and functions of wetlands, riparian, deepwater and related aquatic habitats in priority areas to promote the understanding and conservation of these resources. This data set represents the extent, approximate location and type of wetlands and deepwater habitats in the United States and its Territories. These data delineate the areal extent of wetlands and surface waters as defined by Cowardin et al. (1979). The National Wetlands Inventory - Version 2, Surface Waters and Wetlands Inventory was derived by retaining the wetland and deepwater polygons that compose the NWI digital wetlands spatial data layer and reintroducing any linear wetland or surface water features that were orphaned from the original NWI hard copy maps by converting them to narrow polygonal features. Additionally, the data are supplemented with hydrography data, buffered to become polygonal features, as a secondary source for any single-line stream features not mapped by the NWI and to complete segmented connections. Wetland mapping conducted in WA, OR, CA, NV and ID after 2012 and most other projects mapped after 2015 were mapped to include all surface water features and are not derived data. The linear hydrography dataset used to derive Version 2 was the U.S. Geological Survey's National Hydrography Dataset (NHD). Specific information on the NHD version used to derive Version 2 and where Version 2 was mapped can be found in the 'comments' field of the Wetlands_Project_Metadata feature class. Certain wetland habitats are excluded from the National mapping program because of the limitations of aerial imagery as the primary data source used to detect wetlands. These habitats include seagrasses or submerged aquatic vegetation that are found in the intertidal and subtidal zones of estuaries and near shore coastal waters. Some deepwater reef communities (coral or tuberficid worm reefs) have also been excluded from the inventory. These habitats, because of their depth, go undetected by aerial imagery. By policy, the Service also excludes certain types of "farmed wetlands" as may be defined by the Food Security Act or that do not coincide with the Cowardin et al. definition. Contact the Service's Regional Wetland Coordinator for additional information on what types of farmed wetlands are included on wetland maps. This dataset should be used in conjunction with the Wetlands_Project_Metadata layer, which contains project specific wetlands mapping procedures and information on dates, scales and emulsion of imagery used to map the wetlands within specific project boundaries.

title: Pedestrian Level Traffic Stress
description_raw: Pedestrian Level of Traffic Stress (LTS) models relative levels of roadway walkability based on infrastructure and traffic conditions. Pedestrian LTS is a model for roadway walkability and accessibility based on a weighted average from infrastructure and traffic conditions. These criteria include: lane count, AADT, speed limit, sidewalk presence, sidewalk width, shoulder presence, raised median presence, and roadway illumination. TDOT only has asset data (sidewalks, shoulders, medians) for TDOT-maintained assets, so, roads that lacked this data had those fields marked Null and were given a seperate weighted average based on lane count, AADT, speed limit, and illumination data. Roads which lacked lane count, AADT, or speed limit data were excluded from the analysis.

description_raw: Tennessee roadways with International Roughness Index (IRI) data, which indicates overall roughness of pavements. Lower numbers indicate smoother pavements. This data is for the 2 year cycle of 2022-2023. General Information The International Roughness Index (IRI) defines roughness of pavements in a way that correlates to the movement of a simulated vehicle moving at ~50 mph. Bumps and dips in the pavement which would be experienced by the vehicle driver or rider would increase the IRI. Roughness smaller than a tire footprint that cannot be felt in a vehicle, such as small cracks, should not affect IRI values. The Average Roughness Rating is based on the Average IRI broken down as such: Good - IRI less than 95 Fair - IRI between 95 and 170 Poor - IRI greater than 170 All Interstates and state routes on the National Highway System (NHS) are collected in both directions annually. State routes not on the NHS are collected in one direction every other year. This data is for the 2 year cycle of 2022-2023. Pavement Roughness County Summary Data is provided at the county level; county level summary data does not reflect any one specific roadway or roadway segment.

description_raw: Tennessee roadways with International Roughness Index (IRI) data, which indicates overall roughness of pavements. Lower numbers indicate smoother pavements. This data is for the 2 year cycle of 2022-2023. General Information The International Roughness Index (IRI) defines roughness of pavements in a way that correlates to the movement of a simulated vehicle moving at ~50 mph. Bumps and dips in the pavement which would be experienced by the vehicle driver or rider would increase the IRI. Roughness smaller than a tire footprint that cannot be felt in a vehicle, such as small cracks, should not affect IRI values. The Average Roughness Rating is based on the Average IRI broken down as such: Good - IRI less than 95 Fair - IRI between 95 and 170 Poor - IRI greater than 170 All Interstates and state routes on the National Highway System (NHS) are collected in both directions annually. State routes not on the NHS are collected in one direction every other year. This data is for the 2 year cycle of 2022-2023. This occurs on interstates, state routes, TDOT maintained state park roads, and locally owned NHS routes. No asset data was extracted for these segments of roadway that were under construction. This information was collected using vehicle mounted LiDAR sensors and cameras and was delivered to TDOT by Mandli Communications, Inc. for TDOT needs. This dataset contains lines representing route segments under construction when the asset and photolog vendor collected a route. This occurs on all interstates, state routes, TDOT maintained state park roads, and locally owned NHS routes in Tennessee. No asset data was extracted and delivered for these segments under construction. These records were derived from vehicle mounted LiDAR sensors and digitally captured photos. This information was collected by Mandli Communications, Inc. under the direction of the Asset Management Division and the Long Range Planning Division. Questions on this dataset should be directed to TDOT.Maint.AssetManagement@tn.gov.
